case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a challenge to placement on the federal No Fly List becomes moot when the government removes the plaintiff from the list and represents he will not be relisted based on currently available information, even though the government does not concede the original listing was unlawful.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III, § 2 (Case-or-Controversy requirement; mootness doctrine), applied through the voluntary-cessation exception to mootness.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The government argues the case is moot because Fikre is no longer on the No Fly List and, given the government’s declaration that he will not be placed back on the list based on currently available information, there is no reasonable likelihood of recurrence. Petitioners contend the Ninth Circuit improperly treated the government’s refusal to admit wrongdoing (or to “acquiesce to the righteousness” of Fikre’s position) as a reason to keep the case alive, thereby confusing mootness (a jurisdictional inquiry) with the merits (whether the past listing was justified). They also emphasize a circuit conflict: other circuits (notably the Fourth and Sixth) have treated similar governmental removals and assurances as sufficient to moot prospective claims, and the Ninth Circuit’s approach undermines Article III limits by effectively requiring governmental repudiation to achieve mootness.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Fikre argues the case is not moot under the voluntary-cessation doctrine because the government’s removal decision was made during litigation and its assurance is limited and conditional (tied to “currently available information”), leaving open the possibility of relisting without meaningful constraint. He maintains the government has not carried its “heavy burden” to show it is absolutely clear the challenged conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur. He also contends that continuing harms—especially reputational stigma and related practical consequences tied to being previously labeled a security risk—support continuing justiciability absent a definitive judicial determination or more categorical relief.
key_precedents: Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85 (2013)
Clapper v. Amnesty Int’l USA, 568 U.S. 398 (2013)
City of Mesquite v. Aladdin’s Castle, Inc., 455 U.S. 283 (1982)
Parents Involved in Cmty. Schs. v. Seattle Sch. Dist. No. 1, 551 U.S. 701 (2007)
West Virginia v. EPA, 142 S. Ct. 2587 (2022)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the hardest point: under City of Mesquite, a defendant’s retained discretion plus a conditional assurance (“currently available information”) may be too revocable to satisfy the government’s heavy voluntary-cessation burden. But Mesquite turned on an expressed intent and continuing posture defending reenactment of the very challenged rule, whereas here the Government has taken the concrete step of removing Fikre from the No Fly List and has made a formal representation against relisting on the present record, which—under Already—shifts the inquiry to whether recurrence is reasonably expected rather than theoretically possible. The conditional wording reflects the reality that genuinely new or materially different information could arise; Article III does not require an irrevocable surrender of sovereign authority, only that the asserted future injury be non-speculative, and Justice Alito’s point about the extended period without relisting reinforces that the risk of recurrence on this record is conjectural. A narrow disposition (vacate and remand with instructions to dismiss as moot) best preserves institutional legitimacy by enforcing the case-or-controversy limit without opining on the sensitive merits of the listing regime.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s best point is that the Government’s assurance is conditional (“currently available information”) and therefore, they say, fails the “absolutely clear” burden under City of Mesquite. But Mesquite turned on an expressed intent and ready ability to reenact the very challenged measure; it does not justify treating mere retained discretion—without concrete indicia of imminent relapse—as enough to keep Article III jurisdiction alive. As Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Already instructs that mootness does not hinge on a defendant’s refusal to concede past illegality, and the Ninth Circuit’s focus on non-acquiescence improperly converts a forward-looking jurisdictional inquiry into a merits contest. On this record, the Government’s delisting and formal representation negate any non-speculative likelihood of recurrence, leaving only retrospective disagreement that cannot sustain a live case or controversy.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that the Government’s assurance is conditional (“currently available information”) and thus, under City of Mesquite, too revocable to satisfy the heavy voluntary-cessation burden. But Mesquite turned on an evident willingness to reenact the same challenged policy and thereby a concrete likelihood of recurrence; here, as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, removal from the List plus a formal representation against relisting on the present record makes any future injury depend on genuinely new or materially different intelligence, which is speculative for Article III purposes. Already instructs that mootness does not require a defendant to concede past illegality, and the Ninth Circuit’s approach—treating non-acquiescence as dispositive—improperly converts a forward-looking jurisdictional inquiry into a merits adjudication. Under a practical, consequence-aware application of the case-or-controversy limitation, the absence of any concrete indicator of impending relisting means no live claim for prospective relief remains.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Article III does not require an irrevocable waiver of future sovereign action and that, under Already, the inquiry is practical likelihood of recurrence rather than compelled confession of past illegality. But the government still bears a “heavy burden,” and its assurance—expressly limited to “currently available information”—does not alter the discretionary, opaque relisting machinery in a way that makes it “absolutely clear” recurrence is unreasonable; under City of Mesquite, cessation that is easily reversible by the same decisionmaker with the same authority remains suspect. Justice Alito’s reliance on the passage of time helps on probability, but in a secretive national-security regime where the individual cannot test or even know the evidentiary basis, the asymmetry of information makes the risk of relisting effectively unprovable and thus the government’s conditional promise insufficient to moot. Given the severe liberty consequences of No Fly placement, my pragmatic assessment is that the case remains live for prospective relief.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: the government’s assurance is conditional (“currently available information”) and, under City of Mesquite, voluntary cessation that is easily reversible should not moot a case. But Mesquite’s logic is strongest where the defendant signals an intent or willingness to reenact the challenged practice; here, as the Chief Justice notes, the government has not merely paused conduct but removed Fikre and formally represented it will not relist him on the present record, leaving only a speculative possibility dependent on materially new facts. Under Already’s “absolutely clear” standard, I read the condition as an unavoidable acknowledgement that future intelligence could change, not as a reservation to “return to old ways” on the same facts—so without concrete indicators of impending relisting, the forward-looking equitable controversy has dissipated. I also agree with Justice Roberts that the Ninth Circuit’s focus on non-acquiescence improperly turns mootness into a merits-adjudication about past illegality, contrary to Already’s instruction that mootness is not defeated “no matter how vehemently” past lawfulness is contested.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: under City of Mesquite and the voluntary-cessation doctrine, a defendant’s retained discretion plus a conditional assurance may be “too easily reversible” to moot the case. But Mesquite turned on an evident prospect of reenactment—there, the defendant defended and signaled willingness to restore the challenged rule—whereas here the Government removed respondent from the List and formally represented it will not relist him on the currently available record, leaving only conjecture about future, materially different intelligence. Already, LLC v. Nike refocuses the inquiry on whether recurrence is reasonably expected, “no matter how vehemently” past legality is disputed; the Ninth Circuit’s emphasis on non-acquiescence improperly converts a jurisdictional question into a merits dispute. Article III requires a concrete, non-speculative future injury, and the conditional language merely acknowledges the obvious possibility of genuinely new facts, not a reasonable likelihood of return to the challenged conduct on this record.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: under City of Mesquite, a defendant’s easily reversible cessation—especially where it retains discretion—often fails the “heavy burden” to moot. But Mesquite turned on a live assertion of authority and practical readiness to reenact the very challenged policy; here, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Government removed Fikre from the list years ago and made a formal representation that he will not be relisted on currently available information, which makes recurrence conjectural rather than reasonably expected under Already’s forward-looking inquiry. The conditional language is inevitable in any risk-assessment regime because genuinely new intelligence can arise, and Article III does not require an irrevocable waiver of future sovereign action—only that the complained-of injury is not likely to recur on this record. I also agree with Justice Roberts that the Ninth Circuit’s “acquiescence” focus improperly collapses mootness into a merits adjudication about past listing, leaving at most a retrospective dispute insufficient for prospective equitable relief.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best objection: the Government’s assurance is conditional (“currently available information”) and, they argue under City of Mesquite, too easily reversible to satisfy the heavy voluntary-cessation burden. But Mesquite turned on an expressed intent to reenact the challenged policy, while here—consistent with Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s points—the Government has provided concrete relief (removal) plus a formal representation against relisting on the current record, leaving only speculation that genuinely new facts might arise. Under Already, the Article III question is whether recurrence is reasonably expected, not whether the defendant has bound itself against all conceivable future action or conceded past illegality; the Ninth Circuit’s “acquiescence” focus improperly converts jurisdiction into a merits adjudication. The conditional wording reflects the reality that future intelligence could materially change, but absent any record evidence indicating likely relisting, that theoretical possibility does not keep a live controversy over prospective relief.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is that Already forbids turning mootness on the Government’s refusal to concede past illegality and asks instead whether recurrence is reasonably expected; I agree the Ninth Circuit’s “acquiescence” framing is wrong. But their conclusion still does not satisfy the Government’s “heavy burden” because the assurance is expressly contingent (“currently available information”) and leaves the same discretionary, opaque relisting machinery fully intact, which—under City of Mesquite—makes cessation too revocable to render it “absolutely clear” the challenged restraint cannot reasonably be expected to recur. Justice Alito’s reliance on seven years of non-relisting helps on likelihood, yet in this secretive national-security setting the individual cannot test whether the predicate has truly been abandoned, and the practical consequences of relisting are so severe that a conditional, non-binding representation is inadequate to extinguish prospective equitable jurisdiction. On a pragmatic Article III view focused on real-world incentives and enforceable constraints, the Government has not shown it cannot readily “return to its old ways,” so the controversy over forward-looking relief remains live.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III requires a live case or controversy, and under the voluntary-cessation doctrine a case becomes moot if it is “absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur.” Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). Here, the government removed respondent from the No Fly List years ago and has represented he will not be relisted based on currently available information, which—absent concrete evidence of likely relisting—satisfies the recurrence inquiry and makes the dispute over the original listing’s legality insufficient to preserve jurisdiction. The Ninth Circuit erred by treating the government’s refusal to concede wrongdoing as dispositive, because Already makes clear mootness can exist “no matter how vehemently the parties continue to dispute the lawfulness” of the precipitating conduct. A narrow disposition vacating and remanding for dismissal as moot best serves institutional legitimacy by enforcing Article III’s limits without reaching the merits of the listing procedures.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III limits the federal judicial power to live “Cases” and “Controversies,” and when the challenged prospective restraint has ended, a plaintiff must show a non-speculative likelihood of recurrence to avoid mootness. Under Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., a case becomes moot if it is “absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur,” and that conclusion holds “[n]o matter how vehemently the parties continue to dispute the lawfulness of the conduct that precipitated the lawsuit.” Here, the Government removed Fikre from the No Fly List and represented he will not be relisted based on currently available information; the Ninth Circuit erred by treating the Government’s refusal to concede past illegality as jurisdictionally dispositive, thereby collapsing mootness into the merits. Absent concrete evidence (not mere conjecture) that relisting is reasonably likely, the dispute over past listing is not a justiciable case or controversy under U.S. Const. art. III, § 2.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III limits our jurisdiction to live controversies, and a claim for prospective relief becomes moot when it is "absolutely clear" the challenged conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur. Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). Here, the government has removed Fikre from the No Fly List and, for more than seven years, has not relisted him; coupled with its representation that it will not relist him based on currently available information, that history is strong evidence that recurrence is not reasonably likely. Already also makes clear that mootness does not turn on whether the defendant concedes past illegality—"[n]o matter how vehemently the parties continue to dispute the lawfulness of the conduct"—so the Ninth Circuit erred by treating the government’s failure to repudiate the prior listing as keeping the case alive, rather than focusing on forward-looking recurrence under Article III.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III mootness is not satisfied where the defendant’s voluntary cessation leaves it not “absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur.” Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). The government’s assurance here is conditional—limited to “currently available information”—and it offers no binding constraint comparable to a change in law, leaving open the practical possibility of relisting and thus failing to meet its heavy burden under the voluntary-cessation exception. City of Mesquite v. Aladdin’s Castle, Inc., 455 U.S. 283 (1982), teaches that courts do not treat such easily reversible changes as mooting a case, particularly where the defendant retains discretion to resume the challenged conduct. Given the severe, liberty-restricting impacts of No Fly placement and the need for meaningful judicial review for those most vulnerable to erroneous designation, the case should proceed notwithstanding the government’s refusal to concede past unlawfulness.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III mootness turns on whether there remains a live dispute about prospective relief, and under the voluntary-cessation doctrine the case is moot if it is “absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur.” Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). The Ninth Circuit erred by treating the government’s refusal to concede the past listing was unlawful as dispositive, because mootness does not require “acquiesce[nce] to the righteousness” of the plaintiff’s position; parties may dispute past legality even when no forward-looking injury remains. On this record, removal from the No Fly List plus an executive representation that Fikre will not be relisted based on currently available information suffices to eliminate a reasonable likelihood of recurrence, and any remaining reputational or retrospective concerns do not sustain equitable jurisdiction absent a continuing restraint. U.S. Const. art. III, § 2.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III confines us to live cases and controversies, and voluntary cessation moots a claim for prospective relief when it is “absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur.” Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). Here the government has removed Fikre from the No Fly List and formally represented he will not be relisted on the basis of currently available information; under Already, a defendant’s failure to concede past unlawfulness does not keep a case alive “no matter how vehemently the parties continue to dispute the lawfulness” of what occurred. The Ninth Circuit’s emphasis on the government’s refusal to “acquiesce” improperly collapses a jurisdictional inquiry into a merits dispute, contrary to Article III’s separation-of-powers limits. Absent concrete evidence—not speculation—of likely relisting, the prospective challenge is moot.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Article III’s case-or-controversy requirement, a claim for prospective relief becomes moot upon voluntary cessation if it is “absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur.” Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). Here, the government removed Fikre from the No Fly List and provided a formal representation that he will not be relisted based on currently available information; the Ninth Circuit erred by effectively requiring the government to concede past unlawfulness, because mootness turns on the likelihood of recurrence “no matter how vehemently the parties continue to dispute the lawfulness” of past conduct. Id. at 91. On this record, the asserted risk of relisting is too speculative to sustain jurisdiction, and the remaining dispute over the propriety of the prior listing is a merits question rather than a basis to avoid mootness.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III permits jurisdiction only over a live case or controversy, and claims for prospective equitable relief become moot when it is “absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur.” Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). On this record, the government’s removal of Fikre from the No Fly List coupled with its formal representation that he will not be relisted based on currently available information eliminates any non-speculative threat of future injury, and Article III does not require the government to concede past unlawfulness to moot forward-looking claims. The Ninth Circuit erred by treating the government’s refusal to “acquiesce” in Fikre’s view of the merits as dispositive; Already makes clear mootness turns on future recurrence “no matter how vehemently the parties continue to dispute the lawfulness of the conduct that precipitated the lawsuit.” U.S. Const. art. III, § 2; Already, 568 U.S. at 91.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Article III’s voluntary-cessation doctrine, the government bears a “heavy burden” to show it is “absolutely clear” the challenged conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur. Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). The government’s assurance—limited to “currently available information”—is conditional and leaves meaningful room for relisting based on later-developed or recharacterized intelligence, a concern this Court has treated as sufficient to defeat mootness where a defendant remains free to “return to his old ways.” City of Mesquite v. Aladdin’s Castle, Inc., 455 U.S. 283, 289 (1982). Given the No Fly List’s severe practical consequences and the lack of a categorical, binding commitment that Fikre will not be relisted absent materially changed circumstances or procedural safeguards, I would hold the case not moot and allow judicial review to ensure procedural fairness.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Yonas Fikre’s challenge to his past placement on the No Fly List remains a live Article III case for prospective equitable relief after the government removed him from the list and issued assurances about future non-placement, or whether the claims are moot under the voluntary-cessation doctrine.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III (Case-or-Controversy requirement; mootness doctrine as applied through voluntary cessation).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The government argues the case is moot because Fikre is no longer on the No Fly List and the government has provided a declaration that, based on currently available information, he will not be placed on the No Fly List in the future. Under Article III, courts may not decide disputes once there is no longer a live controversy, and voluntary-cessation principles are satisfied here because recurrence is not reasonably likely. The Ninth Circuit, the government contends, wrongly required the government to “acquiesce” in Fikre’s view that his original listing was unlawful (i.e., to repudiate past conduct) to establish mootness—confusing mootness (forward-looking likelihood of recurrence) with the merits (whether the past listing was justified). The government also emphasizes a circuit conflict (particularly with the Fourth and Sixth Circuits) and argues the Ninth Circuit’s approach improperly keeps national-security list challenges alive even when prospective risk has abated.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Fikre argues the case is not moot under the voluntary-cessation doctrine because removal from the No Fly List during litigation, coupled with a conditional, information-dependent assurance, does not make it “absolutely clear” the challenged conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur. He contends the government retains discretionary authority to relist him, has not conceded the original listing was wrongful, and thus could revert to the challenged conduct. He also frames continuing injury as including stigma and practical consequences associated with having been listed, and maintains that absent a stronger repudiation or binding constraint on future relisting, the court can still grant meaningful relief (e.g., declaratory or injunctive relief preventing future relisting on the same grounds).
key_precedents: Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85 (2013)
City of Mesquite v. Aladdin’s Castle, Inc., 455 U.S. 283 (1982)
West Virginia v. EPA, 142 S. Ct. 2587 (2022)
Parents Involved in Community Schools v. Seattle School District No. 1, 551 U.S. 701 (2007)
Clapper v. Amnesty International USA, 568 U.S. 398 (2013)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Thomas correctly emphasize Laidlaw and City of Mesquite’s “heavy burden” and the Government’s qualified assurance (“currently available information”), but those cases turned on record evidence of likely reenactment or strategic backsliding, not the mere retention of authority. Here, as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch note, the years-long delisting and an on-the-record representation make any recurrence depend on genuinely new, unknown facts, which renders the asserted future injury too conjectural under Clapper to keep Article III jurisdiction alive. Justice Jackson’s reliance on West Virginia v. EPA properly restates the demanding mootness standard, yet it cannot be applied so rigidly that executive discretion alone defeats mootness—otherwise mootness would be functionally unattainable whenever the Government could theoretically act again. Consistent with Already, I would resolve this narrowly: the Ninth Circuit erred by effectively conditioning mootness on repudiation of past conduct rather than assessing the practical likelihood of recurrence and the forward-looking redressability of relief on this record.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito correctly stress that Article III forbids advisory opinions about past illegality and that speculative chains of events cannot sustain jurisdiction under Clapper, but that argument does not answer the distinct voluntary-cessation inquiry. Laidlaw and City of Mesquite place a “heavy burden” on the party asserting mootness to show it is “absolutely clear” the challenged conduct cannot reasonably recur, and the Government’s assurance—expressly limited to “currently available information” and leaving officials free to relist—lacks the kind of binding, operative effect that mooted the case in Already. Justice Kagan’s contention that relisting would require “genuinely new facts” is not a record-based constraint on executive discretion; it is a prediction, and under our mootness doctrine the Government must do more than forecast good behavior. Under a strict Article III analysis faithful to our precedents, the case remains live because prospective relief could still redress a non-foreclosed risk of recurrence.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Thomas are right to emphasize Laidlaw and City of Mesquite’s “heavy burden,” and the Government’s phrasing (“currently available information”) is not ideal. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, those voluntary-cessation cases turned on concrete indicia of likely reenactment or strategic backsliding, whereas here recurrence depends on genuinely new, unknown facts plus discretionary judgments, which is too conjectural under Clapper to keep Article III jurisdiction alive. Justice Jackson’s reliance on West Virginia v. EPA restates the demanding mootness standard, but it cannot be read to mean that the Executive’s retained authority alone defeats mootness; that would make mootness nearly unattainable in contexts where the Government necessarily preserves discretion. And I agree with Justice Gorsuch that the Ninth Circuit’s approach effectively demands repudiation of past conduct, which Already rejects because it converts mootness into a merits concession and invites advisory opinions—especially problematic in sensitive national-security designations.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the strongest point that Article III cannot be satisfied by a desire to adjudicate past illegality, and that under Clapper the feared future harm cannot rest on speculative chains. But those principles do not displace Laidlaw and City of Mesquite’s voluntary-cessation rule: the Government bears a heavy burden to make it “absolutely clear” recurrence cannot reasonably be expected, and its assurance—expressly limited to “currently available information” and preserving unilateral discretion to relist—falls short of the binding, legally operative commitment that mooted the case in Already. Unlike the petitioners’ framing, the conditionality here is not merely factual humility; it signals the same opaque mechanism can be redeployed without durable constraints, so prospective relief remains meaningfully redressive rather than advisory. West Virginia v. EPA, as Justice Jackson notes, reinforces insisting on a truly live controversy, and on this record the controversy remains live because the challenged restraint has not been made practically impossible to resume.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Thomas raise the best objection: Laidlaw/City of Mesquite place a heavy burden on a defendant invoking voluntary cessation, and the Government’s “currently available information” qualifier lacks the unconditional, legally operative force of the covenant in Already. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, our mootness inquiry is practical and forward-looking—whether recurrence is reasonably expected on this record—not a demand that the Executive disclaim all future authority; otherwise retained discretion alone would defeat mootness in virtually every government case. Here, years of nonlisting plus an on-the-record representation mean any relisting would hinge on genuinely new facts and intervening judgments, making the asserted future injury too contingent under Clapper to keep Article III jurisdiction alive. Justice Jackson’s West Virginia v. EPA point reinforces that we must avoid adjudicating abstract disputes, and on this record the Ninth Circuit’s approach risks converting the “absolutely clear” standard into ongoing judicial supervision absent concrete indicia of likely relisting.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Thomas properly emphasize Laidlaw and City of Mesquite’s “heavy burden” and the Government’s qualified assurance (“currently available information”), but those precedents still ask a practical, forward-looking question: whether recurrence is reasonably expected on this record, not whether the Executive has surrendered all future authority. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, years of non-relisting plus an on-the-record representation makes any future injury turn on genuinely new facts and discretionary judgments, rendering the asserted recurrence too contingent to preserve a live Article III case under Clapper. Justice Jackson’s reliance on West Virginia v. EPA restates the demanding mootness standard, yet it cannot be read to make retained discretion alone defeat mootness; that would effectively erase mootness and invite advisory opinions about past actions—precisely what Already warns against by rejecting a “repudiation” requirement. Under a textualist/originalist Article III approach, the Ninth Circuit’s rule improperly prolongs jurisdiction absent a concrete likelihood of the same challenged conduct recurring.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Thomas are right to press that Laidlaw and City of Mesquite impose a heavy burden and that the Government’s assurance is qualified by “currently available information.” But as the Chief Justice explains, those voluntary-cessation cases featured concrete record evidence of likely reenactment or strategic backsliding, whereas here the years-long delisting plus an on-the-record representation make any recurrence depend on genuinely new and unknown facts, rendering the asserted future injury too contingent under Clapper. Justice Jackson’s reliance on West Virginia v. EPA underscores that we must insist on a truly live dispute, yet it does not mean the Executive’s mere retention of legal authority forever defeats mootness; reading “absolutely clear” that way would erase mootness for government defendants and invite advisory opinions. Already reinforces that the Ninth Circuit’s approach effectively demands repudiation of past conduct, collapsing mootness into the merits and extending Article III beyond its practical, precedent-bound limits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Thomas rightly emphasize Laidlaw and City of Mesquite’s “heavy burden” and the Government’s qualifier (“currently available information”), and that point has real force because voluntary cessation cannot rest on a strategically revocable promise. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan argue, those precedents still ask a practical, forward-looking Article III question—whether recurrence is reasonably expected on this record—not whether the Executive has surrendered all future statutory authority; otherwise, retained discretion would categorically defeat mootness and effectively erase the doctrine in suits against the Government. Here the years-long delisting plus an on-the-record representation make the feared injury contingent on genuinely new, unknown facts, bringing the case closer to Clapper’s prohibition on speculative chains and to Already’s insistence that federal courts do not adjudicate past illegality absent meaningful prospective redress. I would therefore reject the Ninth Circuit’s apparent “repudiation” requirement as collapsing mootness into a merits confession and keep my vote for mootness on this record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is that years of nonlisting plus an on-the-record representation make recurrence depend on new facts and thus “speculative” in the Clapper sense, and that Already cautions against turning mootness into a demand for repudiation. But that argument elides the voluntary-cessation posture: under Laidlaw and City of Mesquite the Government bears a “heavy burden” to make it “absolutely clear” the challenged conduct cannot reasonably recur, and a statement expressly limited to “currently available information” leaves the same discretionary, opaque relisting machinery fully intact. Unlike Already’s legally operative, unconditional covenant that removed the restraint, this record supplies no durable, binding constraint that would make recurrence practically impossible, so prospective relief remains meaningfully redressive rather than advisory. Under a pragmatic, procedural-fairness lens—especially given the severe real-world consequences of relisting—the Government’s retained discretion here is not a theoretical possibility but a live, unmitigated risk that defeats mootness.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III mootness turns on whether it is “absolutely clear” the challenged conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur, not on whether the defendant concedes past illegality. Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013), makes clear that a dispute over the lawfulness of past conduct does not keep a case alive once prospective relief can no longer redress a likely future injury. Here, Fikre has been off the No Fly List for years and the government has provided an assurance that, based on currently available information, he will not be relisted, making the risk of recurrence too speculative to sustain forward-looking equitable relief under Article III (cf. Clapper v. Amnesty Int’l USA, 568 U.S. 398 (2013)). For institutional legitimacy and narrow decisionmaking, the Court should resolve the case on mootness grounds and reject the Ninth Circuit’s apparent requirement that the government “repudiate” its past conduct to obtain mootness.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III’s case-or-controversy requirement demands mootness only when it is “absolutely clear” the challenged conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur, and the party asserting mootness bears that “heavy burden.” Under City of Mesquite v. Aladdin’s Castle and Laidlaw, the Government’s voluntary removal of Fikre from the No Fly List during litigation—paired with an assurance expressly contingent on “currently available information” and leaving officials free to relist—does not make recurrence sufficiently impossible to extinguish prospective equitable claims. Already, LLC v. Nike illustrates that mootness may follow where a defendant’s commitment is broad and binding enough to eliminate any live dispute; the Government’s declaration here is not the functional equivalent of such an unconditional covenant. Because the Government retains ongoing discretionary authority to reimpose the challenged restriction, the controversy over prospective relief is not moot under Article III.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III requires a live case or controversy, and a claim for prospective equitable relief becomes moot when it is “absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur.” Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). Here, the government has removed Fikre from the No Fly List and provided an assurance, based on currently available information, that he will not be relisted; the Ninth Circuit erred by effectively demanding a repudiation of past conduct, which Already expressly says is unnecessary for mootness “no matter how vehemently” the parties dispute legality. Absent non-speculative evidence of likely relisting, keeping the case alive would extend the voluntary-cessation doctrine beyond its text and practical limits and would improperly entangle courts in forward-looking supervision of sensitive national-security determinations. U.S. Const. art. III therefore bars further adjudication of prospective relief on this record.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Article III, voluntary cessation moots a claim for prospective equitable relief only if it is “absolutely clear” the challenged conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur, and the burden rests with the party asserting mootness. Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). The government’s removal of Fikre from the No Fly List, paired with an assurance expressly conditioned on “currently available information” and leaving intact the government’s discretionary authority to relist, does not satisfy that demanding standard and resembles the kind of reversible posture this Court has been wary of in City of Mesquite v. Aladdin’s Castle, Inc., 455 U.S. 283 (1982). Given the severe, practical stakes for an individual’s ability to travel and the risk of repeat injury without a binding constraint, the case remains live for forward-looking relief under the voluntary-cessation doctrine.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III requires a live controversy for prospective equitable relief, and under the voluntary-cessation doctrine a case is moot when it is “absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur.” Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). Here, the government’s removal of Fikre from the No Fly List years ago, combined with a formal declaration that he will not be relisted based on currently available information, is sufficient to eliminate a reasonable likelihood of recurrence; insisting that the government also repudiate the past listing conflates mootness with merits, which Already rejects (“[n]o matter how vehemently” the parties dispute legality). Unlike City of Mesquite v. Aladdin’s Castle, 455 U.S. 283 (1982), there is no concrete indication the government is poised to reenact the same challenged conduct, and a generalized possibility of future relisting based on new information is too speculative to sustain jurisdiction under Article III.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III limits us to live cases and controversies, and under the voluntary-cessation doctrine a claim for prospective equitable relief becomes moot when it is “absolutely clear” the challenged conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur. Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). Here, the government removed Fikre from the No Fly List years ago and provided a sworn assurance that, on the currently available information, he will not be placed back on it—making any feared recurrence speculative rather than imminent, which cannot sustain jurisdiction. The Ninth Circuit erred by effectively requiring the Executive to concede past unlawfulness to establish mootness, a merits inquiry Already expressly rejects as irrelevant to Article III mootness.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Article III requires a live case or controversy, and a claim for prospective equitable relief becomes moot when it is “absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur.” Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). Here, the government’s removal of Fikre from the No Fly List and its formal assurance that, based on currently available information, he will not be relisted substantially reduces any concrete likelihood of recurrence, and the Ninth Circuit erred by effectively demanding the government concede past unlawfulness—a merits question Already says is irrelevant to mootness. Absent a non-speculative showing of likely relisting (cf. Clapper v. Amnesty Int’l USA, 568 U.S. 398 (2013)), continued litigation would amount to an advisory opinion about past conduct rather than forward-looking relief, contrary to Article III’s limits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III requires a live case or controversy, and a claim for prospective equitable relief becomes moot when it is “absolutely clear the allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur.” Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). Here, respondent has been off the No Fly List for years and the government has provided an on-the-record declaration, which substantially reduces any non-speculative likelihood of recurrence; mere conjecture that the Executive could relist him is insufficient to avoid mootness. City News & Novelty, Inc. v. City of Waukesha, 531 U.S. 278, 283 (2001). The Ninth Circuit erred to the extent it effectively required the government to concede the past listing’s unlawfulness to establish mootness, because voluntary-cessation analysis turns on forward-looking recurrence rather than a merits repudiation. Already, 568 U.S. at 91.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Article III, voluntary cessation moots a claim for prospective equitable relief only when the defendant shows it is “absolutely clear” the challenged conduct “could not reasonably be expected to recur.” Already, LLC v. Nike, Inc., 568 U.S. 85, 91 (2013). Here, the government’s assurance is expressly contingent on “currently available information” and does not bind the government’s broad discretion to relist, so it falls short of the stringent Laidlaw/Parents Involved standard reaffirmed in West Virginia v. EPA, 142 S. Ct. 2587, 2607 (2022). Given the severe practical consequences and procedural-fairness concerns surrounding secretive listing decisions, a live controversy remains about whether prospective relief is needed to prevent relisting on the same or similarly unsupported grounds.
